newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FOCUS - Kuwait Oil Tanker Co to make record profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kuwait Oil Tanker Co to make record profit.

text.p: Kuwait Oil Tanker Co (KOTC), surviving two Gulf wars and embezzlement, said on Monday net profit for the fiscal year to end-June would reach a record 18 million dinars ($60 million).

"Actual net profit until March was 14 million dinars and for the first time in the company's history we are expecting a record 18 million dinars by the end of the (fiscal) year," KOTC's Sheikh Salman al-Sabah told Reuters.
Net profit for the previous year was 8.5 million dinars, added Sheikh Salman, deputy managing director for administration and finance.

About 55 percent of the 1996/97 profit came from shipping operations while the sale of three ageing ships, shares in a local shipyard and return on cash deposits accounted for the rest, said Rashed al-Shadad, manager of budget and costs.

KOTC, which carries about 20 percent of Kuwait's exports of crude and oil products, suffered heavy losses during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war when its vessels were repeated targets for Iran, angered by the tiny Gulf state's firm political and financial support for fellow Arab Iraq.

The firm moved to the United Arab Emirates from Kuwait when Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait in 1990, chartering most of its fleet to Saudi Arabia which swiftly raised its crude output to make up for lost Iraqi and Kuwaiti exports.
The company -- which now operates 29 crude, product and gas carriers -- was then hit by a financial scandal costing more than $100 million and triggering a major restructuring.

"For the first time we will internally finance the purchase of the two new crude carriers without any help" from Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC), the state mother company which runs the country's oil sector, said Sheikh Salman.
In December KOTC ordered two 309,000-tonne crude tankers from South Korea's Hyundai Industries Co worth a total $160 million. They are due for May and June 1998 delivery.
KOTC officials refused to disclose the size of its cash holdings but said return on investment for 1996/97 was $4.0 million. The state firm is only allowed to make bank deposits.
The new vessels will have a double hull to meet American environmental regulations which industry experts say would eventually be adopted by Europe.
KPC currently charters vessels to carry its exports to the United States while KOTC carriers deal mainly with Kuwait's customers in Asia and Europe.
KOTC has several studies for fleet replacement and possibly raising total tonnage to keep pace with Kuwait's plan to raise crude production capacity and environmental requirements.

"Our fleet is ageing and about half of our vessels are 10 to 16 years old. There are studies to renew the fleet, taking into consideration KPC's marketing expansion," said Sheikh Salman of Kuwait's plans to raise its crude production capacity by 100,000 barrels per day to 2.5 million bpd in the next few years.
Kuwait, which has an OPEC quota of two million bpd, hopes to reach a production capacity of three million bpd by 2005.

KOTC Chairman Abdullah al-Roumi told Reuters "there is a plan which has not been finalised yet and we could start moving on it early next year." He was referring to a possible requirement for several 80,000 tonne products tankers.

Company officials attributed some of the rise in net profit to better management, including a drop in hull, machinery and protection and indemnity insurance to $8.9 million for the current fiscal year from $18.9 million in 1993/94.
"We broke the British monopoly (as KOTC's sole insurance provider) and opened new insurance markets bringing in the French and others," said Faisal Ali, manager insurance group.

Sheikh Salman stressed that KOTC was not receiving any KPC handouts or favouritism with all charter deals between the two concluded at market price. "We are a profit centre not a cost centre," he added proudly.
